title: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) older adults vaccination coverage in England: June 2026 report - gov.uk

analysis.time: Published 6 August 2026; data period 1 September 2024 to 30 June 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: England; eligible older adults (routine cohort: individuals turning 75 on or after 1 September 2024; catch-up cohort: individuals aged 75–79 before 1 September 2024).
analysis.event: Official statistics report on respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccination uptake among older adults in England, published by the UK Health Security Agency.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Overall vaccine uptake among eligible older adults reached 63.5% by 30 June 2026; catch-up cohort uptake 69.2%, routine cohort 48.3%. Regional variation: highest in South West (68.3%), lowest in London (49.4%). Uptake by sex: males 65.4%, females 61.7%. By deprivation: most deprived decile 50.3%, least deprived 71.6%. By ethnicity: highest in White-British (67.0%), lowest in Asian or Asian British-Pakistani (25.1%). By ICB: highest in NHS Bath and North East Somerset, Swindon and Wiltshire (70.5%), lowest in NHS North East London (46%).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Report designated as official statistics; cumulative uptake data presented monthly; programme ongoing with dynamic eligibility for routine cohort; regional, demographic, and ethnic disparities noted; no explicit risk assessment provided in the evidence.

analysis.brief_en: The UK Health Security Agency reported on 6 August 2026 that 63.5% of eligible older adults in England had received an RSV vaccine by 30 June 2026 under the national immunisation programme launched on 1 September 2024. Coverage was higher in the catch-up cohort (69.2%) than in the routine cohort (48.3%), reflecting the programme’s staged rollout to those aged 75–79 before the start date and those turning 75 thereafter. Regional uptake ranged from 68.3% in the South West to 49.4% in London, with notable disparities by sex, deprivation, ethnicity, and integrated care board area. The report, designated as official statistics, tracks cumulative uptake monthly and highlights persistent inequities in access to vaccination among older populations.

Regional uptake ranged from 68.3% in the South West to 49.4% in London, with notable disparities by sex, deprivation, ethnicity, and integrated care board area. The report, designated as official statistics, tracks cumulative uptake monthly and highlights persistent inequities in access to vaccination among older populations.

title: RSV-B Resistance to Nirsevimab Detected in Breakthrough Infections - EMJ

analysis.location_and_population: France; infants aged one year or younger with laboratory-confirmed RSV infection.
analysis.event: First large-scale real-world evidence of nirsevimab-resistant RSV-B variants detected in breakthrough infections; study authors emphasize resistance remains confined to breakthrough cases.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 1,023 infant RSV cases sequenced; 419 breakthrough infections in nirsevimab recipients and 439 in non-recipients; 12.5% of RSV-B breakthrough infections carried resistance (vs 1.0% in RSV-A); no resistant strains detected in untreated infants; overall clinical effectiveness of nirsevimab remains high despite resistance emergence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Multicentre POLYRES-2 observational study; genomic surveillance combined with neutralisation testing; authors recommend integrating genomic sequencing into routine surveillance to monitor emerging escape mutations and guide future monoclonal antibody development; resistant variants can persist beyond the immediate RSV season.

analysis.brief_en: A nationwide observational study in France has detected nirsevimab-resistant respiratory syncytial virus B (RSV-B) variants in infants with breakthrough infections during the 2024–2025 RSV season. Among 1,023 infants with confirmed RSV, 419 had received nirsevimab prophylaxis and 439 had not. Resistance was identified in 12.5% of RSV-B breakthrough cases, primarily involving substitutions at residue 208 of the viral F protein, while only 1.0% of RSV-A breakthrough infections showed resistance. Crucially, no resistant strains were found in untreated infants, indicating resistance emerged under selective pressure from prophylaxis. The authors stress that resistance remains confined to a minority of breakthrough infections and does not signal widespread treatment failure, but they call for expanded genomic surveillance to track viral evolution and inform future monoclonal antibody design.
analysis.summary_en: A nationwide observational study in France has detected nirsevimab-resistant respiratory syncytial virus B (RSV-B) variants in infants with breakthrough infections during the 2024–2025 RSV season. Among 1,023 infants with confirmed RSV, 419 had received nirsevimab prophylaxis and 439 had not. Resistance was identified in 12.5% of RSV-B breakthrough cases, primarily involving substitutions at residue 208 of the viral F protein, while only 1.0% of RSV-A breakthrough infections showed resistance. Crucially, no resistant strains were found in untreated infants, indicating resistance emerged under selective pressure from prophylaxis. The authors stress that resistance remains confined to a minority of breakthrough infections and does not signal widespread treatment failure, but they call for expanded genomic surveillance to track viral evolution and inform future monoclonal antibody design.

title: U.S. FDA Accepts sBLA for ENFLONSIATM (clesrovimab-cfor) to Update its Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Lower Respiratory Tract Disease Indication to Include Children Under ...

analysis.time: The FDA accepted the sBLA on August 6, 2026, with a PDUFA date set for March 22, 2027. The Phase 3 SMART trial results were published in September 2025 and July 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) are involved. The target population is children under two years of age at increased risk for severe RSV disease, including those with chronic lung disease, congenital heart disease, or early/moderate preterm birth.
analysis.event: The FDA accepted a supplemental Biologics License Application (sBLA) for ENFLONSIATM (clesrovimab-cfor) to expand its indication to include prevention of RSV lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) in children under two years of age during their second RSV season. This is supported by data from the Phase 3 SMART trial.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: ENFLONSIATM is approved in over 40 countries for use in infants during their first RSV season. The trial included 502 infants in RSV season 1 and 276 in RSV season 2, with 99% of season 2 participants having chronic lung disease or congenital heart disease. The drug is intended to reduce the burden of RSV on families and healthcare systems.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The FDA has accepted the sBLA, and the EMA has accepted the application for the EU. The trial data supports the regulatory filings, and the drug is currently approved in multiple countries. The response is ongoing with further regulatory filings in progress.

analysis.brief_en: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has accepted a supplemental Biologics License Application (sBLA) for ENFLONSIATM (clesrovimab-cfor) to expand its indication to include prevention of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) in children under two years of age at increased risk for severe RSV disease during their second RSV season. This decision is supported by data from the Phase 3 SMART trial (MK-1654-007), which was presented at RSVVW’26 and published in the New England Journal of Medicine and JAMA Pediatrics. The FDA has set a PDUFA date of March 22, 2027, for a decision. The EMA also accepted the application for the European Union in July 2026. ENFLONSIATM is the first and only preventive option for RSV LRTD in infants without weight-based dosing. It is approved in over 40 countries, including the U.S., Canada, the EU, China, and Japan, for use in infants during their first RSV season. The drug is designed to provide protection for up to five months, a typical RSV season, and is administered within the first week of life for infants born during the RSV season. The trial included 502 infants in RSV season 1 and 276 in RSV season 2, with 99% of season 2 participants having chronic lung disease or congenital heart disease. The regulatory filings aim to further reduce the burden of RSV on families and healthcare systems.

analysis.time: Published on 2026-08-02. No specific event date is reported in the evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: Global, with specific focus on infants, older adults, and vulnerable populations such as premature babies, children with underlying diseases, and leukemia patients.
analysis.event: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is a leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections in children under five and poses a persistent threat to child health worldwide. Early-infancy infection with RSV significantly increases the risk of developing childhood asthma, especially in children with a family history of allergy or asthma. RSV also causes severe outcomes and heart complications in older adults.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: RSV leads to high hospitalization rates in adults, with a large real-world randomized trial in Denmark finding that the RSVpreF vaccine reduced RSV-related hospitalizations in adults aged 60 and over by over 80%. A single dose of the RSV vaccine offers 58% protection against hospitalization in older adults, but effectiveness varies in immunocompromised individuals. Year-round access to RSV immunization may reduce major seasonal outbreaks across the nation.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Pediatric experts are preparing for an expected rise in cases of RSV during the respiratory virus season. Maternal vaccination and nirsevimab together offer complementary strategies to protect newborns during their highest-risk months. The World Health Organization (WHO) has published its first-ever position paper on immunization products to protect infants against RSV. However, HEPA purifiers do not fully reduce classroom viral exposure, suggesting additional interventions are needed.

analysis.brief_en: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) remains a significant global health threat, particularly affecting infants and older adults. Early RSV infection in infancy increases the risk of childhood asthma, especially in children with a family history of allergy or asthma. For older adults, RSV causes severe outcomes and heart complications, with vaccines showing effectiveness in reducing hospitalizations by over 80% in adults aged 60 and over. Maternal vaccination and nirsevimab provide complementary protection for newborns during their highest-risk months. The WHO has issued its first position paper on RSV immunization for infants, emphasizing the need for year-round access to immunization to minimize seasonal outbreaks. Despite these advances, additional interventions are needed as HEPA purifiers alone do not fully reduce classroom viral exposure.
analysis.summary_en: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) remains a significant global health threat, particularly affecting infants and older adults. analysis.brief_en: On August 6, 2026, Merck announced that the U.S. FDA accepted a supplemental Biologics License Application for ENFLONSIATM (clesrovimab-cfor) to expand its RSV lower respiratory tract disease indication to include children under two years at increased risk for severe RSV during their second season. title: Rsv season approaches as doctors urge infant protection

analysis.time: Published on 2026-08-10; event timing inferred as approaching fall respiratory virus season (N1).
analysis.location_and_population: United States, Shreveport area, Louisiana; target population: infants and newborns (N2, N3, N7).
analysis.event: Public health guidance issued by a family medicine physician (Dr. David Janese) urging parents to protect infants from RSV ahead of the upcoming respiratory virus season (N3, N6, N7).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: RSV is described as the most common virus putting newborns at risk for pneumonia and airway inflammation; no case counts, deaths, or exposures reported in the supplied evidence (N3).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Physicians recommend consulting pediatricians about RSV vaccinations and maintaining a germ-free environment; parents advised to seek medical care if infants show fever, trouble breathing, or reduced responsiveness (N5, N11). Current status: preventive guidance under dissemination; no outbreak investigation details reported (N5, N11).

analysis.brief_en: As fall approaches, U.S. physicians are urging heightened protection for infants against Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), the leading cause of pneumonia and airway inflammation in newborns. Dr. David Janese, a family medicine physician with Ochsner LSU Health in Shreveport, Louisiana, highlights new preventive options, including vaccinations, and advises parents to consult their child’s pediatrician. Experts emphasize keeping infants’ environments germ-free and seeking immediate medical attention if symptoms such as fever, breathing difficulties, or lethargy arise. While RSV season looms, no specific case counts or outbreaks are detailed in the guidance, which focuses on proactive measures to shield the most vulnerable.

title: Nirsevimab Immunization Outcomes in the First Two Years - Bioengineer.org

analysis.time: Published 2026-08-10; study covers 2023–2024 and 2024–2025 RSV seasons with outcomes assessed during the first two years after administration.
analysis.location_and_population: Infants and young children, particularly those born prematurely or with underlying medical conditions, in settings where RSV circulates seasonally.
analysis.event: A study published in JAMA Pediatrics reported that nirsevimab, a long-acting monoclonal antibody, was associated with a substantial reduction in hospitalizations due to RSV-related lower respiratory tract infections during the first year after administration.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study observed substantially fewer RSV-related hospitalizations in children who received nirsevimab compared to those who did not during the first year of follow-up across two consecutive RSV seasons. No reduction was observed in hospitalizations from non-RSV infections or asthma, indicating a pathogen-specific effect. The benefit did not extend to the second year.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study is observational and demonstrates an association rather than definitive causation. Differences in treatment decisions, underlying health, birth history, healthcare access, and other characteristics may influence results. The protective effect is limited to the first year, and older children face a lower risk profile. Findings complement clinical trial evidence by showing real-world performance across multiple seasons.

analysis.brief_en: A study published in JAMA Pediatrics reports that nirsevimab, a long-acting monoclonal antibody, significantly reduced hospitalizations from RSV-related lower respiratory tract infections in infants during the first year after administration. The protective effect was consistent across the 2023–2024 and 2024–2025 RSV seasons, with substantially fewer admissions among treated children compared to untreated peers. The benefit was specific to RSV and did not extend to non-RSV infections or asthma-related hospitalizations. Protection waned by the second year, aligning with the antibody’s designed duration of action. Researchers emphasize that while the findings support real-world effectiveness, the study’s observational design limits causal inference and unmeasured factors may influence outcomes.

title: Q&A: Which Hospitalized Children With RTIs Face the Highest Risk for Severe Disease? - Physician's Weekly

analysis.location_and_population: Two Canadian pediatric centers: The Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto, Ontario) and BC Children’s Hospital (Vancouver, British Columbia); 2,585 hospitalized children with acute respiratory tract infections (RTIs), median age 2.5 years.
analysis.event: Retrospective cohort study reporting that more than one in five hospitalized children developed severe disease; highest risk observed in children transferred from a referring hospital, those with multiple chronic conditions, infants under 1 year, and adolescents over 10 years. Findings published in JAMA Network Open and discussed by an external expert.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 2,585 enrolled children; 551 (21.3%) met severe illness criteria including cardiac arrest, need for noninvasive or invasive ventilation, ECMO, or kidney replacement therapy; 37 (6.7% of severe cases) died. Chronic conditions (especially neurologic, developmental, or genetic) and transfer status were associated with increased risk; viral coinfections (≈15%) were not associated with severity.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Study authors recommend targeted prevention, ongoing surveillance, and prioritizing RSV prevention strategies for medically complex children. Findings emphasize patient-specific risk factors over viral diagnosis alone and highlight challenges in interpreting highly sensitive molecular tests. No active public-health response actions are described in the report.

analysis.brief_en: A retrospective cohort study of 2,585 Canadian children hospitalized with acute respiratory tract infections (RTIs) between July 2022 and June 2023 found that more than one in five developed severe disease, with 21.3% requiring intensive interventions and 6.7% of severe cases ending in death. Risk was highest among infants under one year, adolescents over ten years, children transferred from another hospital, and those with multiple chronic conditions—particularly neurologic, developmental, or genetic disorders. Respiratory syncytial virus and enterovirus-rhinovirus were the most commonly detected pathogens, but viral coinfections did not increase severity. Experts recommend closer monitoring and earlier escalation for high-risk patients, alongside routine immunizations and RSV-targeted prevention where indicated.
analysis.summary_en: A retrospective cohort study of 2,585 Canadian children hospitalized with acute respiratory tract infections (RTIs) between July 2022 and June 2023 found that more than one in five developed severe disease, with 21.3% requiring intensive interventions and 6.7% of severe cases ending in death. Respiratory syncytial virus and enterovirus-rhinovirus were the most commonly detected pathogens, but viral coinfections did not increase severity. Experts recommend closer monitoring and earlier escalation for high-risk patients, alongside routine immunizations and RSV-targeted prevention where indicated.
